title: Why He Scratched Cow Pus Into a Boy
topic: Why Edward Jenner scratched cowpox into a boy's arm in 1796

lines: A doctor scratched cow pus into an eight-year-old boy's arm.
The boy was James Phipps, the gardener's son.
The doctor was Edward Jenner, in England, 1796.
Jenner was a country doctor in Berkeley.
Smallpox killed one in ten people around the world.
In crowded towns, it killed one in five.
Jenner had been inoculated for smallpox himself as a boy, and it wrecked his health for life.
Doctors at the time used smallpox itself to protect people.
They scratched smallpox pus into a healthy person's skin.
That person usually got a milder case and survived.
But sometimes they got full smallpox and died.
And they could spread smallpox to everyone around them.
You see, it's like fighting fire with fire, hoping the fire doesn't burn down your house.
Jenner wanted something safer.
He had heard that milkmaids who caught cowpox never seemed to get smallpox.
Cowpox was a mild disease you caught from cows.
On May fourteenth, 1796, Jenner scraped pus from cowpox blisters on the hands of Sarah Nelmes, a milkmaid.
She had caught cowpox from a cow called Blossom.
Jenner scratched that pus into James Phipps's arm.
The boy got mildly sick, then recovered.
Then Jenner did something bolder.
He scratched actual smallpox into the boy.
James Phipps did not get sick.
The cowpox had protected him.
Jenner called his method vaccination, from the Latin for cow.
He proved it with more cases in 1798.
The British government banned the old risky method in 1840 and gave out cowpox vaccine for free.
The world's first vaccine was born from a milkmaid, a cow named Blossom, and a gardener's son.

claims.claim: In 1796, Jenner scratched cowpox pus into James Phipps, the eight-year-old son of his gardener.
Jenner scraped pus from cowpox blisters on the hands of Sarah Nelmes, a milkmaid who caught cowpox from a cow called Blossom.
In Jenner's time, smallpox killed around 10% of the global population, up to 20% in towns and cities.
Jenner was inoculated for smallpox as a boy, which had a lifelong effect on his health.
Variolation used smallpox itself, scratched into the skin, and usually caused a milder infection but could spread smallpox to others.
In 1840, the British government banned variolation and provided cowpox vaccination free of charge.
Jenner's 1798 work showed the vaccine maintained effectiveness through at least four serial arm-to-arm transfers.
